title: Her Masterpiece Ended Up on a Horse's Grave.

brand.cta: Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

beats.text: Her masterpiece ended up on a horse's grave.

overlays.hook: Her masterpiece *ended up on a horse's grave.*

beats.text: Born in New York around 1844, to a Black father and an Ojibwe mother, she was orphaned young.
At Oberlin College, two white classmates said she had poisoned them. She was beaten. The charges were dropped.
She became a sculptor, and moved to Rome to carve white marble.
In 1876, she sent The Death of Cleopatra, two tons of marble, to the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia.
It drew bigger crowds than almost anything else in the hall.
Then it vanished. It turned up in a Chicago saloon. A racetrack owner bought it to mark his horse's grave. The horse was named Cleopatra.
Covered in graffiti, it ended up in a salvage yard.
A local historical society rescued and restored it. In 1994, they gave it to the Smithsonian.
Today, her Cleopatra is on view in Washington.

facts.claim: Born c. 1844 in upstate New York to a free Black father and an Ojibwe/Chippewa mother; orphaned young.
1862 at Oberlin: accused of poisoning two white roommates; beaten by vigilantes; charges dismissed / acquitted.
Settled in Rome among expatriate American sculptors, worked in marble.
The Death of Cleopatra shown at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition, Philadelphia; marble, about two tons (Yale unit) / nearly three tons (Wikipedia).
People's Advocate: it 'excites more admiration and gathers larger crowds' than other works in Memorial Hall.
Lost for nearly a century; décor in a Chicago saloon; a racetrack owner (Blind John Condon) bought it to mark the grave of his horse Cleopatra.
Graffiti removed in restoration; found in a salvage/storage yard (late 1970s or 1980s).
Restored by the Historical Society of Forest Park, given to the Smithsonian American Art Museum in 1994.
